lessons.title: Get to Know After Effects
objectives: State what After Effects costs monthly in shillings and what hardware it genuinely needs, and name the free alternatives if either is out of reach
Explain compositions, layers and the project file as references rather than copies, so missing footage stops being a mystery
Say what After Effects is not - a video editor - and set a composition's frame rate and resolution correctly before animating anything
lessons.notes:
After Effects is a compositor and animation tool. Before learning any of it, two practical facts decide whether this is your path.

THE COST, PLAINLY

It is SUBSCRIPTION ONLY. There is no one-off purchase. You pay every month, in dollars, on a card that works for cross-border payments, and the software stops working when you stop paying.

Convert the current monthly price to shillings at today's rate, add your card's cross-border fee, and multiply by twelve. Write that number down. For most learners here it is a serious recurring commitment, and it should be a decision rather than a default.

THE HARDWARE, HONESTLY

After Effects is one of the heaviest applications an ordinary person runs:

- RAM IS THE BINDING CONSTRAINT. 8 GB is painful and will have you waiting on previews constantly. 16 GB is the realistic minimum for comfortable work. More helps directly, and more RAM is almost always the cheapest upgrade that makes the biggest difference.
- A SOLID-STATE DRIVE for the disk cache. On a mechanical drive, previewing is slow in a way no setting fixes.
- A GRAPHICS CARD helps some effects and does nothing for others. Do not buy one expecting a general speed-up.
- SCREEN SPACE. The interface wants room. On a small laptop screen you will spend real time rearranging panels.

If your machine is below that, you are not blocked from motion graphics. You are blocked from this particular application.

THE FREE ALTERNATIVES, WHICH ARE REAL

- DAVINCI RESOLVE has a genuinely capable free version, and its Fusion page does compositing and motion graphics. It is NODE-based rather than layer-based, which is a different way of thinking but not a worse one. Many professionals prefer it.
- BLENDER is free, and besides 3D it has a video sequencer and a compositor. Already deep in this catalogue as its own course.
- CAPCUT AND CANVA handle simple animated text and templates. If what a client actually needs is a title on a clip, these finish the job in ten minutes.

Choose by what you will be asked to produce. A learner whose paid work is animated titles for local businesses does not need a dollar subscription to deliver it.

THE MENTAL MODEL: COMPOSITIONS, LAYERS, TIME

A COMPOSITION is a container with a size, a frame rate and a duration. Everything happens inside one. You can nest a composition inside another, which is how complicated work stays manageable.

A LAYER is one element inside a composition - a video clip, an image, a piece of text, a shape, a solid colour, a camera, a light. Layers stack: upper layers sit in front of lower ones.

The extra dimension is TIME. In a still-image editor a layer has a position. Here it has a position AT EVERY MOMENT, and animation is the record of how that value changes. That is the whole idea, and the next lesson is about doing it well.

It is LAYER-based, not node-based. Each layer carries its own effects and transforms, read bottom to top. Resolve's Fusion builds a connected graph instead. Neither is wrong; knowing which you are in stops a great deal of confusion.

THE SETTING THAT RUINS WORK SILENTLY: FRAME RATE

A composition has a frame rate - frames per second - set when you create it. Get it wrong and the symptoms are subtle and maddening: motion that stutters slightly, exported video that does not match the footage it was cut with, audio drifting out of sync over a long piece.

The rule: MATCH THE COMPOSITION TO THE FOOTAGE AND TO THE DELIVERY. If your source clips are 25 fps and the final video is 25 fps, the composition is 25 fps. Mixing rates needs deliberate handling, not hope.

Resolution works the same way. Set the composition to the dimensions you will deliver - and if you will deliver to several places, read the aspect-ratio section of lesson 5 before you start, because reframing afterwards is far more work than planning for it.

THE PROJECT FILE REFERENCES MEDIA, IT DOES NOT CONTAIN IT

This surprises every beginner once. Your project file is small because it holds instructions, not video. The actual clips, images and audio live wherever they live on disk, and the project only points at them.

So if you move, rename or delete a source file, the project opens with colour bars and a missing-footage warning. Nothing is corrupted; the pointer broke.

The discipline that prevents it:

- ONE FOLDER PER PROJECT, with subfolders for footage, audio, graphics and exports.
- Put every asset inside that folder BEFORE importing it. Never import from a downloads folder or a phone.
- Never rename a source file after importing.
- When you move the project to another machine, move the whole folder.

AFTER EFFECTS IS NOT A VIDEO EDITOR

It can cut clips, badly and slowly. Editing a twenty-minute video in it is a mistake people make once.

The right division of labour: cut and arrange in an editor, then bring individual shots into After Effects for the work only it can do - animated graphics, titles, compositing, effects - and send the result back. For short pieces that are entirely graphics, staying here the whole way is fine.

PREVIEW, CACHE AND WHY NOTHING PLAYS SMOOTHLY AT FIRST

Playback is not real time until the frames have been computed and stored. As it plays, the composition builds a cache; the second playthrough of the same section is smooth because it is replaying stored frames.

Two consequences to accept early: the first pass over new work will be slow, and the cache consumes real disk space in a folder you should point at your fastest drive. Lesson 6 is entirely about making this bearable.

WHAT TO LEARN FIRST, AND WHAT TO IGNORE

There are hundreds of effects and you need almost none of them. The useful order:

1. Keyframes and easing - lesson 2, and the one that actually determines whether your work looks professional.
2. Text animators - lesson 3.
3. Shape layers and their modifiers - lesson 4, which does most real motion-graphics work.
4. Masks, track mattes and parenting.
5. Only then expressions, 3D and the effect library.

People reverse this, learn forty effects, and still produce animation that moves like a lift. The order above is the difference.
lessons.practice:
Decide whether this is your tool, then set one project up so it cannot break.

Step 1. Price it honestly:

- Current monthly subscription in dollars: ____
- At today's rate, in shillings: ____
- Plus card cross-border fee: ____
- Twelve months: KSh ____

Step 2. Check your machine against the notes and write each line:

- RAM: ____
- Drive type: ____
- Screen size: ____
- Your honest verdict: comfortable, painful, or not viable: ____

If the verdict is not viable, write which free alternative you will learn instead and why. That is a legitimate outcome of this lesson, not a failure.

Step 3. Build the folder before the project. Make one project folder with subfolders for footage, audio, graphics and exports. Write the path.

Step 4. Put two assets INSIDE that folder, then import them. Create a composition and write down the three settings you chose:

- Width by height: ____
- Frame rate, and the footage frame rate it matches: ____
- Duration: ____

Step 5. Break it on purpose, then fix it. Close the project, rename one source file, reopen. Observe the missing-footage warning. Then rename it back and confirm it relinks. Write one sentence on what the project file actually stores.

Step 6. Animate one property - move a layer from one side to the other - and play it back twice. Write down how long the first playthrough took to become smooth, and why the second was faster.

Step 7. Point the disk cache at your fastest drive and note how much space you allowed it.

Step 8. Write your learning order as a list of five items, from the notes, and name the one you will NOT touch until the other four are solid.

quiz.question: You open yesterday's project and see colour bars with a missing-footage warning. What happened?
options: The project file is corrupted and must be rebuilt
The project stores references to media rather than the media itself, so a moved or renamed source file breaks the pointer
The subscription lapsed
The composition frame rate changed

quiz.question: Your laptop has 8 GB of RAM and a mechanical hard drive. What is the honest assessment?
options: After Effects will run comfortably once effects are disabled
Motion graphics is out of reach entirely
This application will be painful, but motion graphics is not blocked - a free node-based alternative is a reasonable route
Buying a graphics card will solve it

lessons.title: Keyframe Animation Basics
objectives: Describe a keyframe as a value at a time, and explain why the interpolation between keyframes is what makes motion look good or mechanical
Use easing and the graph editor to control speed over time, rather than accepting linear motion
Apply anticipation, overshoot, follow-through and offset timing, which are what separate professional motion from amateur motion
lessons.notes:
This is the most important lesson in the course. Everything else is buttons; this is the craft. Animation that looks amateur almost never fails because of the effects used. It fails here.

WHAT A KEYFRAME ACTUALLY IS

A keyframe records a VALUE at a TIME. Position is 100 at frame 0; position is 500 at frame 24. Two keyframes.

The software then fills in every frame between them. That filling-in is called INTERPOLATION, and it is the whole subject. The keyframes are your intention; the interpolation is what the viewer sees.

WHY LINEAR MOTION LOOKS WRONG

By default the fill-in is LINEAR: constant speed from start to finish, then an instant stop. Nothing in the physical world moves like that. A hand reaching for a cup accelerates and decelerates. A door swings and settles. A dropped phone speeds up.

Linear motion reads as robotic, and it is the single most recognisable mark of a beginner. Fixing it costs one keystroke and transforms the work.

EASING: THE FIRST FIX

Easing changes how speed is distributed between two keyframes:

- EASE OUT of the first keyframe: start slowly, build speed. Good for something beginning to move.
- EASE IN to the last keyframe: arrive slowly, settle. Good for something stopping.
- EASE BOTH, which is the default choice for most moves and already looks ten times better than linear.

Apply easing to every move you make, then decide whether that particular move wants something different. Starting from eased and removing it is better practice than starting from linear and forgetting.

THE GRAPH EDITOR: WHERE THE ACTUAL CONTROL IS

The graph editor shows interpolation as a curve you can shape. Beginners avoid it because it looks mathematical. It is the single highest-value thing in this application.

Two views, and knowing which you are looking at matters:

- THE VALUE GRAPH plots the property's value against time. A straight diagonal line means constant speed.
- THE SPEED GRAPH plots how fast the value is changing. A flat line means constant speed; a hill means accelerate then decelerate.

What to do with it:

- Drag the handles at each keyframe to steepen or flatten the curve. A steep middle with flat ends is a fast move that starts and ends softly - which describes most good motion.
- For a snappy, modern feel: very fast at the start, then a long slow settle. That asymmetry is most of what people mean by "snappy".
- For weight: a heavy object accelerates slowly and takes longer to stop. Shape the curve and the object gains mass without you drawing anything.

Spend an hour in the graph editor and your work will improve more than from a month of learning effects.

THE FOUR PRINCIPLES THAT DO THE REST

Borrowed from traditional animation and all cheap to apply:

ANTICIPATION. Before something moves one way, it moves slightly the other way first. A character crouches before jumping. A logo pulls back a few pixels before flying in. Two or three frames is enough, and it makes motion feel intentional rather than teleported.

OVERSHOOT. The object goes slightly PAST its final position, then comes back. This is the most useful single trick in motion graphics - it is what makes text and shapes feel alive. Keep it small; a few pixels on a small element, more on a large one.

FOLLOW-THROUGH. Parts of a thing do not stop at the same instant. If a card flies in and stops, its shadow or a trailing element arrives a frame or two later. Nothing in reality arrives all at once.

OFFSET TIMING. When several things animate, do NOT start them together. Stagger them by two to four frames. A row of five icons appearing simultaneously looks dead; the same five staggered looks designed. This one principle fixes more amateur work than any other.

TIMING AND SPACING, WHICH ARE DIFFERENT

TIMING is how long a move takes - the number of frames. SPACING is how the distance is distributed across those frames.

Two moves of the same duration can feel completely different depending on spacing, and spacing is what the graph editor controls. When something feels wrong but you cannot say why, it is almost always spacing.

HOW LONG SHOULD A MOVE BE?

Useful starting ranges, to be broken deliberately:

- A small interface-style move: 8 to 15 frames.
- A significant element entering: 15 to 25 frames.
- A dramatic reveal: 30 frames or more.
- Anything over about 45 frames needs a reason, or the viewer waits.

At 25 frames per second, 12 frames is about half a second. Count in frames, not in feelings.

THE ANCHOR POINT, AND THE COMMONEST FRUSTRATION

Rotation and scale happen around the ANCHOR POINT. If a layer rotates in a way you did not expect, the anchor is not where you assumed - often at the centre when you wanted a corner, or left behind at the original position after you moved the layer.

Move the anchor point itself rather than fighting the result. This small thing causes a disproportionate share of beginner frustration.

PARENTING AND NULLS

Parent one layer to another and it inherits the parent's transforms. Animate the parent and the children follow.

A NULL is an invisible layer that exists only to be a parent. Animate a null and twenty layers move together, while each keeps its own independent animation on top. This is how complicated scenes stay editable, and it is worth learning before your first project with more than five elements.

WHEN NOT TO KEYFRAME BY HAND

If you are placing forty keyframes to make something wobble, stop. There are expressions and modifiers that generate that motion from a few parameters, and they stay adjustable afterwards while forty hand-placed keyframes do not. You do not need expressions yet - just recognise the signal: repetitive keyframing means there is a better way.
lessons.practice:
Run the comparison that teaches this, then apply the four principles.

Step 1. Animate one square moving across the screen with two keyframes, left to right, over 20 frames. Watch it. This is linear motion.

Step 2. Duplicate the layer and apply easing to both keyframes on the copy. Play them one after the other. Write one sentence describing the difference. Keep both; this pair is your reference for the rest of the course.

Step 3. Open the graph editor on the eased version. Drag the handles to make the move very fast at the start and slow to settle. Play it. Write which of the three versions you would use in paid work and why.

Step 4. Switch between the value graph and the speed graph on the same keyframes. Write one line describing what each one is showing you.

Step 5. Add anticipation. Before the move begins, shift the square 10 pixels in the OPPOSITE direction over 3 frames. Play it.

Step 6. Add overshoot. Let it travel about 20 pixels past the final position, then come back over 5 frames. Play it. Write which of anticipation and overshoot changed the feel more.

Step 7. Prove offset timing. Make five squares in a row. Animate them all starting on the same frame. Watch it. Then stagger their start times by 3 frames each. Watch again. Write one sentence - this is the single biggest lesson in the course.

Step 8. Fix the anchor point deliberately. Rotate a rectangle around its centre, then move the anchor to one corner and rotate again. Write what changed.

Step 9. Use a null. Parent your five squares to a null, animate the null moving up, and confirm all five follow while keeping their own staggered animation. Write why this is better than animating five layers.

Step 10. Count in frames. For each of your moves, write the frame count and whether it falls in the ranges from the notes.

quiz.question: Your animation looks mechanical even though the positions are correct. What is the most likely cause?
options: The composition resolution is too low
The keyframes use linear interpolation, so speed is constant and stops instantly - easing and the graph editor are the fix
Too few effects have been applied
The anchor point is wrong

quiz.question: Five icons appear on screen and the result looks lifeless. What single change helps most?
options: Make the move longer
Add a drop shadow to each icon
Stagger their start times by a few frames each instead of starting them together
Increase the frame rate of the composition

lessons.title: Animating Text: The Write-On Effect
objectives: Animate text per character with text animators and range selectors, rather than keyframing letters by hand
Build a write-on reveal with a mask or a trim path, and know which approach suits which source
Make text readable on a phone and legally usable in client work: size, contrast, hold time and font licensing
lessons.notes:
Animated text is the most common paid motion-graphics job there is: titles, lower thirds, captions, adverts. It is also where the two failures that matter most happen - unreadable text and an unlicensed font.

TEXT ANIMATORS: THE FEATURE WORTH LEARNING

Keyframing each letter by hand is how beginners animate text, and it is unmaintainable: change the word and the work is gone.

TEXT ANIMATORS do it properly. You add an animator for a property - position, opacity, scale, rotation, blur, colour - and a RANGE SELECTOR decides WHICH characters it currently affects. Animate the range selector, and the effect sweeps through the text.

So a word fading in letter by letter is TWO keyframes on the range selector's start value, not one per letter. Change the text and the animation still works. That difference is the whole reason to learn this.

Three range-selector settings that change everything:

- UNITS: percentage or index. Percentage adapts when the text length changes; index counts actual characters.
- BASED ON: characters, words or lines. Word by word is usually better for a sentence that must be READ; letter by letter suits a short title.
- SMOOTHNESS and the EASE HIGH/LOW values, which soften the boundary so characters do not pop in abruptly.

THE WRITE-ON EFFECT, TWO WAYS

Both produce handwriting appearing as though drawn. Which you use depends on what you have.

WITH A MASK AND A STROKE. Draw a mask path along the stroke of the letters, apply a stroke effect that follows the path, and animate its end from 0 to 100 percent while set to reveal the layer underneath. This is the classic approach and it works on any artwork, including a scanned signature or a hand-drawn logo. It is fiddly: complicated letterforms need several paths, and the result is only as good as the paths.

WITH A SHAPE LAYER AND TRIM PATHS. If the lettering is vector - from a vector drawing application, or text converted to shapes - trim paths animate the stroke drawing itself, cleanly, with no masking. Far less work and much better quality, which is why the next lesson treats trim paths as a core tool.

The practical rule: if you can get the lettering as vector, use trim paths. If all you have is a raster image of handwriting, use the mask-and-stroke method.

READABILITY, WHICH DECIDES WHETHER ANY OF IT WORKED

Most of your viewers are watching on a phone, often small and often held at arm's length, and they will not rewind. Text they cannot read in the time available has failed regardless of how well it animated.

So:

- HOLD IT LONG ENOUGH TO READ TWICE. Read it aloud at a comfortable pace, double that, and that is your minimum hold. Beginners hold text for a second and wonder why nobody absorbed it.
- MAKE IT BIGGER THAN FEELS NECESSARY on your monitor. Preview at phone size - shrink the preview window until it is roughly the size of a phone screen - and judge it there. This single habit fixes most title design.
- CONTRAST, NOT JUST COLOUR. Light text on a light video is unreadable. Put a subtle dark shape or gradient behind text over footage; it looks deliberate and it solves the problem.
- SHORT LINES. A title is not a paragraph. If it does not fit in two lines, it is a different piece of content.
- STAY INSIDE A SAFE MARGIN. Keep text well away from the frame edge: platforms crop, overlay interface elements on top of your video, and a caption at the very bottom disappears behind a play bar or a username.
- ANIMATE IN, THEN STOP. Text that keeps moving while it is meant to be read is unreadable. Animate on, hold perfectly still, animate off.

FONTS ARE LICENSED, AND THIS MATTERS IN CLIENT WORK

A font downloaded free from a font site is often licensed for PERSONAL USE ONLY. Using it in work a client pays for, or in anything advertising a business, can be a breach of the licence - and foundries do pursue it.

Protect yourself:

- Read the licence before using a font in paid work. The words to look for are "commercial use".
- Prefer fonts whose licence is unambiguous: open-licensed families from large free libraries, or fonts included with a subscription you already pay for.
- When a client gives you a font, ask whether they hold the licence. If they do, keep their confirmation in writing.
- Keep a note per project of which fonts you used and under what licence. A year later nobody remembers.

And the practical point: the font file must be installed on whatever machine opens the project. Hand a project to somebody without the font and the text reflows into a substitute, which silently ruins careful layout. Either supply the font with the licence that permits it, or convert the text to shapes before handing over.

LANGUAGE, HERE

Much of the work you will do is in English, Swahili or both. Two things follow:

- Swahili words are often longer than their English equivalents. A title that fits on one line in English may wrap in Swahili, which breaks the layout and the timing. Design for the longer version.
- If a video mixes languages, keep the typographic treatment consistent so the switch does not look like a different video.

THE ORDER TO BUILD A TITLE IN

1. Set the text and get the type size and line breaks right, at phone size, before animating anything.
2. Add the background shape if it is needed for contrast.
3. Animate ON with a text animator, 10 to 20 frames, eased.
4. HOLD, perfectly still, long enough to read twice.
5. Animate OFF, usually faster than the entrance.

Beginners animate first and design second, then spend an hour adjusting keyframes around text they then change anyway.
lessons.practice:
Build one lower third properly and test it where it will be watched.

Step 1. Write the text first. Two lines maximum, in the language you will actually deliver. Then write the Swahili version and check whether it still fits.

Step 2. Set the type at a size that reads when you shrink the preview to roughly phone size. Note the font size you ended on, and how it compares with what looked right at full screen.

Step 3. Add a background shape or gradient behind the text and place it over real footage. Write one line on the contrast before and after.

Step 4. Animate it on using a TEXT ANIMATOR, not hand keyframes. Use an opacity or position animator with a range selector, and write down:

- Units: percentage or index, and why
- Based on: characters, words or lines, and why
- Frames the entrance takes: ____

Step 5. Prove the animator was worth it. Change the wording completely. Confirm the animation still runs correctly without being rebuilt. Write what happened.

Step 6. Set the hold. Read the text aloud at a comfortable pace, time it, double it, and hold for that long with NO movement. Write both numbers.

Step 7. Build a write-on both ways on a short word:

- Mask plus stroke on a raster image of handwriting
- Trim paths on vector lettering

Write which took longer and which looked better.

Step 8. Check the safe margin. Move the lower third away from the frame edge and write how much space you left, remembering platform interface overlays.

Step 9. Settle the font licence. Write the font name, where you got it, and the exact licence terms on commercial use. If you cannot find the terms, choose a different font and say so.

Step 10. Export a short clip and watch it on an actual phone, at arm's length, once, without rewinding. Write down whether you could read it, and the one change you made because of that.

quiz.question: Why animate text with a text animator and range selector instead of keyframing each letter?
options: It renders faster
Because the animation is defined independently of the characters, so changing the wording does not destroy the work
It allows more effects per layer
Hand keyframes cannot animate opacity

quiz.question: You used a font downloaded free from a font website in a paid advert for a client. What should you have checked?
options: That the font file is under 1 MB
That the font supports your frame rate
The licence terms on commercial use, since many free fonts are licensed for personal use only
Nothing - free fonts carry no restrictions

lessons.title: Shape Layers and Motion Graphics
objectives: Build vector shape layers that scale without quality loss, and navigate the group structure that confuses beginners
Use trim paths, the repeater and offset path to produce motion without keyframing each element
Explain the difference between a layer transform and a shape-group transform, and why one rotates differently from the other
lessons.notes:
Shape layers are where most real motion-graphics work happens. They are vector, they are generated inside the application, and their modifiers produce in two clicks what would otherwise be fifty keyframes.

VECTOR, WHICH MEANS NO QUALITY LOSS

A shape layer is defined by paths, strokes and fills - mathematics, not pixels. Scale it to 400 percent and the edges stay perfectly sharp. The same thing done to an imported image goes soft.

This is the same raster-versus-vector distinction the illustration course teaches, met from the other side, and it has a direct practical consequence: build graphic elements as shape layers rather than importing them as images whenever you can, because you will be asked to deliver at a different size eventually.

THE GROUP STRUCTURE, AND THE CONFUSION IT CAUSES

Open a shape layer's contents and the nesting is deeper than people expect: the layer contains groups, each group contains a path, a stroke, a fill, and its own TRANSFORM.

That last one is the thing. There are TWO places to change position, scale and rotation:

- THE LAYER TRANSFORM, in the layer's own properties, which moves the entire layer.
- THE GROUP TRANSFORM, inside the shape contents, which moves only that group within the layer.

They behave differently, and the difference matters most for rotation, because each has its own anchor point. A shape that rotates around the wrong centre is nearly always this: you used one transform when you wanted the other.

The habit that prevents hours of confusion: decide whether you are moving the WHOLE LAYER or ONE SHAPE INSIDE IT, then use the matching transform. And name your groups. An unnamed stack of eight groups is unreadable within a day.

TRIM PATHS: THE LINE-DRAW ANIMATION

Trim paths animate how much of a path is drawn. Animate the END from 0 to 100 percent and a stroke draws itself on. Animate the START after it and the line draws off again.

This single modifier produces:

- A line drawing itself across the screen
- A circle closing as a loading or progress indicator
- Handwriting appearing, far more cleanly than the mask method in the previous lesson
- An underline sweeping in beneath a title
- A map route tracing a journey

Two details worth knowing. The OFFSET property rotates where the trim begins around the path, which is how you make a circle draw from the top rather than the right. And trim paths apply to the GROUP they sit in, so where you place the modifier in the stack decides what it affects.

THE REPEATER: MANY FROM ONE

The repeater duplicates everything in its group a set number of times, applying a transform to each copy in turn - an offset in position, a rotation, a scale, an opacity change.

One square plus a repeater is a row of squares. Add a second repeater and it is a grid. Add rotation instead of position and it is a radial burst or a flower.

Why this matters: you animate the ORIGINAL and every copy follows, and you change the count with one number. Twenty hand-copied layers would be twenty layers to maintain.

The thing people miss: the repeater's own transform can be animated, so the whole pattern can bloom, rotate or scatter from a single keyframed property.

OFFSET PATH, ROUND CORNERS, AND THE REST

- OFFSET PATH grows or shrinks a shape outwards from its own outline. This is exactly the die-cut sticker outline from the illustration course, and here it also makes an outlined version of any shape, animatable.
- ROUND CORNERS softens corners on a path without redrawing it.
- WIGGLE PATHS distorts a path continuously, producing organic motion with no keyframes at all.
- WIGGLE TRANSFORM shakes copies around, which is how you get a crowd of elements that do not look mechanically placed.

Three of those four generate MOTION without a single keyframe. That is the point of this lesson: the modifiers do the repetitive work, and you keep control of a few parameters.

STROKES, FILLS AND DASHES

A group can have several strokes and fills, stacked. Two practical uses:

- A dashed stroke, made with the dash property, animated with trim paths, is the standard animated-route or animated-border look.
- Stroke width can be animated, which gives you a line that thickens as it draws - the single cheapest way to make a line-draw feel hand-made rather than mechanical.

BUILD ONE REUSABLE THING, NOT TEN ONE-OFF THINGS

The practical payoff of this lesson is a LOWER THIRD you keep. Build it once - a shape that trims on, a text layer that animates in, an underline that sweeps - then save it as a composition you duplicate and retype for every future job.

Clients do not pay for you to rebuild a name bar each time. The people who earn from this have a folder of elements they assemble, and they built that folder out of lessons like this one.

AND THE RULE FROM LESSON 2 STILL APPLIES

Everything here still needs easing, offset timing, and a little overshoot. A trim path animating linearly looks as mechanical as anything else. The modifiers decide WHAT moves; lesson 2 decides whether it looks good.
lessons.practice:
Build the elements you will reuse, and settle the transform confusion for good.

Step 1. Make one shape layer with a stroked path. Scale it to 400 percent and look at the edge. Then import a small image and do the same. Write one sentence comparing them.

Step 2. Settle the two transforms. Rotate the shape using the LAYER transform and note what it rotates around. Undo. Rotate it using the GROUP transform inside the shape contents and note the difference. Write one line stating when you would use each.

Step 3. Name every group in your layer. Write down how many there were.

Step 4. Build a trim-path line draw. Animate the end from 0 to 100 over 20 frames, eased. Then use OFFSET to make a circle draw from the top instead of the side. Write the offset value you needed.

Step 5. Use the repeater. Start from one square, set the repeater to 6 copies with a position offset. Then:

- Change the count to 12 with one number and note how long that took
- Animate the original and confirm every copy follows
- Animate the repeater's own transform so the whole pattern rotates

Step 6. Use offset path to make an outlined version of a shape, and animate the offset amount. Write what it looked like.

Step 7. Use wiggle paths on a straight line and write one sentence on how many keyframes that motion required.

Step 8. Make a dashed stroke and animate it with trim paths to produce a route-drawing effect. Then animate the stroke width so the line thickens as it draws.

Step 9. Build a REUSABLE LOWER THIRD combining what you learned: a shape trimming on, text animating in with a text animator from lesson 3, an underline sweeping, all with easing and offset timing from lesson 2. Save it as its own composition in a folder you will keep.

Step 10. Duplicate that lower third and retype it for a different name in under two minutes. If it took longer, write what you would restructure so that it does.

quiz.question: Your shape rotates around a point you did not expect. What is the usual cause?
options: The composition frame rate is wrong
You used the layer transform when you wanted the shape-group transform, or vice versa - each has its own anchor point
The shape needs to be converted to a raster image first
Trim paths are enabled

quiz.question: You need twenty copies of an element arranged in a row, all animating together, with the count easy to change later. What is the right tool?
options: Duplicate the layer twenty times and keyframe each
A repeater on the shape group, which duplicates the contents with a per-copy transform and animates from the original
An expression on each layer's position
Export one copy and re-import it twenty times

lessons.title: Animating a Logo and Title Sequence
objectives: Insist on vector logo artwork, and price the conversion work when a client only has a low-resolution image
Structure a logo sting as build, resolve and hold, at a duration that suits where it will be used
Deliver correctly: the right aspect ratios, the right codec, with or without an alpha channel, named so the client can find them
lessons.notes:
Animating a logo is the commonest first paid motion-graphics job. It is also where beginners lose money, because the problems are not animation problems.

THE FIRST PROBLEM: WHAT THE CLIENT SENDS YOU

You will ask for the logo and receive a small JPEG with a white background, pulled off their own website or lifted from a WhatsApp profile picture. This is normal and you must plan for it.

WHAT YOU ACTUALLY NEED is VECTOR artwork - an AI, EPS, SVG or layered PDF file - because:

- It scales to any size with no quality loss, as lessons 2 and 4 of the illustration course explain.
- Its elements are SEPARATE, so you can animate the mark independently of the wordmark. A flat image cannot be taken apart.
- It has no background baked into it.

So ask, specifically: "Do you have the logo as a vector file - AI, EPS, SVG or PDF? Your designer or printer will have it." Naming the formats and the likely holder gets results far more often than asking for "the original".

If the answer is genuinely no, then REDRAWING THE LOGO AS VECTOR IS A SEPARATE JOB. It takes real time, it requires care to match the original exactly, and it must be quoted and agreed before you start. Doing it silently as a favour sets the expectation that it was free, and it is the commonest way a beginner turns a profitable job into a loss.

THE SECOND PROBLEM: BRAND RULES

Many organisations have brand guidelines, and if they exist you must ask for them. Where they do not, assume these conventions:

- DO NOT RECOLOUR the logo. The colours are the brand.
- DO NOT DISTORT it. Scale proportionally, never stretch one axis.
- DO NOT ROTATE OR FLIP the wordmark unless the guidelines permit it.
- RESPECT CLEAR SPACE. Guidelines usually specify a minimum empty margin around the logo; keep to it in your final held frame.
- DO NOT ADD EFFECTS to the logo itself - no bevels, glows or shadows on the mark - unless asked.

Animating a logo INTO place is fine. Altering the logo is not, and a client whose brand you altered will notice even when they cannot articulate it.

THE STRUCTURE OF A LOGO STING

Three parts, and the third is the one beginners drop:

1. THE BUILD. Elements enter. This is where your craft shows: trim paths drawing the mark, shapes sliding in, text animating with a range selector, everything eased with offset timing.
2. THE RESOLVE. Everything arrives at its final position - the exact, correct, guideline-respecting arrangement of the logo. A small overshoot and settle here is what makes it feel finished.
3. THE HOLD. The complete logo sits perfectly still, long enough to be seen and remembered. At least a second, often more.

Without the hold, the viewer sees movement and never registers the logo, which was the entire purpose. Animating up to the final frame and cutting is the commonest structural error.

DURATION, BY WHERE IT GOES

- A sting at the end of a video: 3 to 5 seconds total, including the hold.
- An opener before content: keep it SHORT, 2 to 3 seconds. Long openers make people leave, and a viewer on a metered connection resents every second of logo before the thing they came for.
- A standalone brand animation for social: 5 to 8 seconds, because it is the content rather than an interruption.

Ask where it will be used before deciding, because the answer changes the brief.

DELIVERABLES: THE PART THAT GETS FORGOTTEN

Agree these in writing BEFORE you start, because each one is work:

ASPECT RATIOS. Where will it play? A video on YouTube is 16:9 wide. An Instagram feed post is square. A story or a reel is 9:16 tall. These are not crops of each other - a logo animation composed for wide will have empty sides when squeezed into tall, and elements that fly in from the left have nowhere to come from.

If the client wants all three, say so in the quote and BUILD FOR IT: compose the animation inside a safe central area, keep elements away from the extremes, and use separate compositions at each size rather than scaling one.

WITH OR WITHOUT A BACKGROUND. An editor who wants to drop your logo over their own footage needs a TRANSPARENT background, which means exporting with an ALPHA CHANNEL - and that requires a codec that supports transparency. An ordinary compressed video file does not carry transparency, and the client will get a black box behind the logo. Ask which they need; deliver both if unsure.

RESOLUTION AND CODEC. Agree the frame size, the frame rate and the file format. A broadcast or agency client may have a specification; a small business wants a file that plays when double-clicked and is small enough to send on WhatsApp.

NAMING. Deliver files a human can identify six months later: client name, what it is, the aspect ratio, the version, the date. A folder of files called Comp 1 final final2 is how clients lose things and come back to ask you again.

VERSIONING YOUR OWN WORK

Save incrementally as you go, with a number on the end, rather than overwriting one file. Two reasons: a client who says "actually the earlier one was better" is a normal event, and a project file that corrupts after four hours of work without an earlier save is a disaster you only need once.

THE QUOTE, SO THIS IS PROFITABLE

Price these as separate lines so the client can see what they are buying:

- Vector redraw, if needed
- The animation itself, for ONE aspect ratio
- Each ADDITIONAL aspect ratio
- A version with alpha channel
- Revision rounds included, and the cost beyond them
- Sound design, if any - and note you need the rights to any music or sound effect you use

That list is the difference between a logo animation that pays and one that quietly consumes a week.
lessons.practice:
Animate one logo end to end, and settle the commercial side first.

Step 1. Write the request you will actually send a client, asking for vector artwork by format name and naming who is likely to hold it.

Step 2. Write your quote, as separate lines with real figures in shillings: vector redraw if needed, animation in one aspect ratio, each additional ratio, alpha-channel version, revision rounds included and cost beyond.

Step 3. Get or make vector artwork for a real logo - a family business, a church, a school. Import it so the mark and the wordmark are SEPARATE and can animate independently. Write how you achieved that.

Step 4. Write the brand rules you will respect: colours unchanged, proportional scaling only, clear space margin, no added effects. Then write where it will be used, because that sets the duration.

Step 5. Build the three parts, with frame counts:

- Build: ____ frames, using trim paths, shapes and a text animator from lessons 3 and 4
- Resolve, with a small overshoot and settle: ____ frames
- HOLD, perfectly still: ____ frames

Confirm the hold is at least a second.

Step 6. Apply lesson 2 properly. Ease every move, stagger the element entrances by a few frames, and add overshoot on the resolve. Write which three keyframes you spent longest shaping in the graph editor.

Step 7. Deliver three aspect ratios: 16:9, 1:1 and 9:16. Build each as its own composition rather than scaling one, and write down what you had to change for the tall version.

Step 8. Export twice: once as an ordinary compressed file, and once with an ALPHA CHANNEL in a codec that supports transparency. Place the second over a coloured background and confirm the transparency survived. Write both file sizes.

Step 9. Name every file so a stranger could identify it: client, what it is, aspect ratio, version, date. Write one filename as an example.

Step 10. Check your own saves. Confirm you have incremental versions rather than one overwritten file, and write how many.

quiz.question: A client sends their logo as a small JPEG with a white background. What is the right response?
options: Animate it as supplied, since it is what they have
Ask specifically for vector artwork by format name and who likely holds it; if there genuinely is none, quote the vector redraw as a separate job before starting
Recolour it to remove the white background and proceed
Scale it up to the delivery resolution and sharpen it

quiz.question: The client's editor needs to place your logo animation over their own footage. What must you deliver?
options: A high-bitrate compressed video, which is enough for any use
The project file so they can render it themselves
An export with an alpha channel in a codec that supports transparency, since ordinary compressed video carries no transparency
A sequence of JPEG images

lessons.title: Speeding Up Your Renders
objectives: Use the disk cache, RAM and pre-rendering deliberately, so previewing stops being the slowest part of your day
Name which effects are expensive, and work with them switched down until the final render
Export at a size that is sensible to upload from Kenya, and survive a power cut mid-render
lessons.notes:
This is the lesson that decides whether you can actually work on the machine you have. Everything here is free and most of it is habit.

UNDERSTAND WHAT IS SLOW AND WHY

Nothing plays in real time until the frames have been computed. Two caches store the results:

- RAM holds recently previewed frames. Fast, and emptied when you close the project.
- THE DISK CACHE holds frames on your drive, so they survive restarts.

Three habits follow:

- POINT THE DISK CACHE AT YOUR FASTEST DRIVE and give it real space - tens of gigabytes if you have them. On a slow drive the cache barely helps.
- PURGE THE CACHE when the application starts behaving oddly or previews show stale frames. It is the first thing to try and it fixes a surprising range of problems.
- CLOSE EVERYTHING ELSE. A browser with twenty tabs is holding gigabytes of RAM that your preview needs. On an 8 or 16 GB machine this is not a marginal gain; it is the difference between previewing and waiting.

PREVIEW SMALLER AND CHEAPER

You do not need full quality to judge timing, and timing is what you are mostly judging:

- DROP THE PREVIEW RESOLUTION to half or a third. Motion reads identically and it previews several times faster.
- REDUCE THE PREVIEW FRAME RATE while roughing out timing.
- PREVIEW ONLY THE SECTION YOU ARE WORKING ON, not the whole composition from the start every time.
- Turn OFF motion blur, depth of field and any 3D while you work, and back on for the final.

THE EXPENSIVE EFFECTS, NAMED

These cost the most per frame, and recognising them tells you where your time is going:

- BLURS AND GLOWS, especially at large radii
- MOTION BLUR, which multiplies the work per frame
- 3D LAYERS with lights and shadows, and depth of field most of all
- PARTICLE SYSTEMS and simulations
- ANYTHING THAT SAMPLES NEIGHBOURING FRAMES - time remapping, frame blending, noise reduction
- NESTED COMPOSITIONS SEVERAL LAYERS DEEP, each one re-rendering on every frame

The working method: build with them switched off or at low settings, judge the motion, then enable them for the final render only.

PRE-COMPOSE AND PRE-RENDER

When a section of your work is FINISHED and heavy, stop recomputing it:

- PRE-COMPOSE to group finished layers into one nested composition. This tidies the timeline, though on its own it does not make rendering cheaper.
- PRE-RENDER the finished section to a file and bring that file back in place of the layers. Now it is a flat clip that costs almost nothing per frame.

Pre-rendering is the single biggest speed gain available on a heavy project, and it is underused because it feels like cheating. It is not; it is how long projects stay workable. Keep the original layers switched off rather than deleted, so a change is still possible.

PROXIES, FOR HEAVY SOURCE FOOTAGE

If your source clips are large - high resolution, or a format that is expensive to decode - make low-resolution PROXY versions and work with those. The application swaps the full-quality originals back in at render time. Your timeline becomes responsive and the final output is unaffected.

EXPORTING, AND THE PART THAT IS SPECIFIC TO HERE

Two routes: the built-in render queue, or sending the composition to a media encoder, which frees the application while it works and offers more delivery presets.

Then the consideration that matters in Kenya and is absent from every tutorial: THE FILE HAS TO GET TO THE CLIENT.

- A near-lossless master is enormous. Uploading a 2 GB file for a client to review is slow, often fails partway, and costs real money in data.
- SO EXPORT TWO FILES: a small compressed version for review, and the high-quality master only once the content is approved. Reviewing a 30 MB file costs almost nothing; reviewing a 2 GB file costs an afternoon and a bundle.
- Choose a widely compatible compressed format for review, at a modest bitrate, at the delivery resolution. If it plays on a phone and the client can see the timing and the words, it has done its job.
- Upload overnight or whenever your connection is least contested, and upload one file at a time.

POWER CUTS, WHICH ARE A REAL PART OF THE WORKFLOW

A render interrupted at 80 percent is a wasted hour, and a project file being written when the power goes can be damaged.

Protect yourself:

- SAVE INCREMENTALLY, as lesson 5 said, and turn on automatic saving at a short interval.
- RENDER IN SEGMENTS on long pieces - several shorter renders instead of one long one - and join them afterwards. A cut then costs you one segment.
- Render during the most reliable hours you have, and if you have a laptop, keep it charged so a render survives a short outage.
- Never let the only copy of a project live on one machine.

THE HONEST SUMMARY

Your machine is probably the constraint, and you cannot fix it with settings alone. What you can do is stop making the machine do unnecessary work: preview small, switch off what you are not judging, pre-render what is finished, close the browser, and export a small file for review.

And when you do upgrade something, RAM first. It is usually the cheapest change and the one you will feel every day.
lessons.practice:
Measure your own machine, then make the same project previewable.

Step 1. Set the disk cache to your fastest drive and allocate real space. Write the drive and the size.

Step 2. Measure the browser cost. With a browser full of tabs open, preview a section and time how long it takes to become smooth. Close everything and repeat. Write both times.

Step 3. Measure preview resolution. Time a preview at full resolution, then at half, then at a third. Write the three times and whether the motion read differently at each.

Step 4. Find your expensive effect. Add a large blur or a glow to a layer and time a preview before and after. Write both numbers, then switch it off and work without it.

Step 5. Pre-render something. Take a finished, heavy section, render it to a file, and bring that file back in place of the layers - keeping the originals switched off rather than deleted. Time a preview before and after. Write both.

Step 6. Make a proxy for your largest source clip and write how the timeline responsiveness changed.

Step 7. Export twice from the same composition:

- A small compressed review file: size ____ MB, upload time ____
- A high-quality master: size ____ MB, estimated upload time ____

Write one sentence on which you would send a client for approval, and why that is not the master.

Step 8. Write your outage plan in four lines: automatic save interval, how you name incremental saves, the segment length you would render a long piece in, and where the second copy of your project lives.

Step 9. Write your preview checklist as five habits you will actually follow, then stick it where you can see it.

Step 10. Write the one hardware upgrade you would make first and what it costs in shillings.

quiz.question: A finished, heavy section of your project makes every preview slow. What gives the biggest speed gain?
options: Pre-composing the layers, which groups them in the timeline
Pre-rendering that section to a file and using the file in place of the layers, so it costs almost nothing per frame
Raising the preview resolution so frames cache properly
Adding more effects to the adjustment layer

quiz.question: A client needs to review your 90-second animation. What should you send?
options: The near-lossless master, so they judge the real quality
The project file and the footage folder
A small compressed version at delivery resolution, keeping the master until the content is approved
A sequence of still frames
